Key Takeaways

  • Organisation is worth up to 24 marks. Use clear paragraphing, topic sentences, and discourse markers to create a coherent, well-structured response.
  • Structural features like opening hooks, circular structure, and one-sentence paragraphs show the examiner you are making deliberate craft choices.
  • Always spend 5 minutes planning. Decide your points, their order, your opening, and your ending before you start writing.

Key Takeaways

  • Every Section B task specifies Purpose, Audience, and Form. Identify all three before writing and let them guide every choice you make.
  • Section B is marked across two strands: Communication and Organisation (24 marks) and VSSP (16 marks). Both content quality and technical accuracy matter.
  • Plan for 5 minutes, write for 40–45 minutes, and check for 5 minutes. A clear structure with discourse markers and varied paragraph lengths shows the examiner you are in control of your writing.

Key Takeaways

  • Summarising means condensing the main ideas of one text into your own words. Synthesising means combining information from two texts to find connections, contrasts, and a fuller picture.
  • Use connective phrases to link the texts explicitly: “Both writers,” “In contrast,” “Whereas,” “Similarly.” These signal genuine synthesis to the examiner.
  • Plan synthesis answers around themes, not texts, to ensure you integrate evidence from both sources in every paragraph.

Key Takeaways

  • Strong openings hook the reader, establish tone, and demonstrate conscious craft — the examiner can predict your grade from your first paragraph.
  • Five effective strategies: in medias res, striking imagery, dialogue, reflective statement, or sensory detail. Avoid alarm clocks, weather clichés, and long backstory.
  • Your opening should connect to your plan — it is the first deliberate move, not an improvised guess.

Key Takeaways

  • Tone is the emotional attitude of the writing, style is the writer’s distinctive use of language, and register is the level of formality. All three must be consistent or deliberately shifted.
  • Decide your tone, style, and register during planning — they determine every vocabulary, sentence, and punctuation choice.
  • The examiner rewards sustained control, not a particular approach. A spare, minimalist style can score just as highly as a rich, lyrical one.
